passages.text: Scope: This note presents the primary concepts needed to understand jeevan: what it is, its five faculties and ten paired activities, how understanding becomes conduct, how delusion differs from awakening, how sanskar is formed, and how the body participates without becoming the knower. A separate technical companion preserves the formal functional model, and the sixty-one-pair inventory preserves the detailed source analysis behind the 122 activities.

Madhyasth Darshan holds that a human being is the joint form of a persistent sentient jeevan and a temporary physicochemical body. Jeevan is the knower and bearer of understanding; the body supplies sensation, neural mediation, speech, skill, and action. Five inseparable faculties organise jeevan’s activity from realisation at atma to selection at mun. Awakening occurs when their activity becomes consonant with understanding and becomes evident in humane conduct.

That account is the darshan’s ontology, not an inference established by contemporary neuroscience. This note first states the textual account and then marks where a cross-text synthesis or functional interpretation begins. It does not reduce jeevan to computation, identify its faculties with brain regions, or treat satta as a commander.

passages.heading: 1-jeevan-knowledge-and-the-human-joint-form
passages.section: 1. Jeevan, Knowledge, and the human joint form
passages.text: 1. Jeevan, Knowledge, and the human joint form

passages.heading: 1-jeevan-knowledge-and-the-human-joint-form
passages.section: 1. Jeevan, Knowledge, and the human joint form
passages.text: Jeevan is a constitutionally complete sentient atom. Its nucleus is named atma; its first, second, third, and fourth orbital groupings are named buddhi, chitta, vritti, and mun. The five are therefore faculties of one unit rather than five agents assembled into a mind (MVD, p. 78; AVD, p. 87). Constitutional completeness releases the atom from molecular and weight bondage while the bondage of hope remains, distinguishing jeevan from physicochemical units without making it inactive (MVD, p. 91).

passages.heading: 1-jeevan-knowledge-and-the-human-joint-form
passages.section: 1. Jeevan, Knowledge, and the human joint form
passages.text: Existence as coexistence is what jeevan can know. Omnipresence, or satta, is Knowledge in the ontological sense: actionless, non-transforming, and available as the ground of law, regulation, balance, justice, dharma, and truth. Knowledge is nevertheless called the basis and source of inspiration for all activity, with inspiration inherent simply because units exist in it (MVD, pp. 32–36, 174). Units act; satta does not.

passages.heading: 1-jeevan-knowledge-and-the-human-joint-form
passages.section: 1. Jeevan, Knowledge, and the human joint form
passages.text: Every unit, including jeevan, exists submerged, soaked, and surrounded in satta. This standing condition is called saturation and is what “coexistence” names at the ontological level (MVD, p. 32). Realisation belongs to atma, and knowledge becomes humanly evident through the joint form of jeevan and body. Reading inspiration as the standing availability of reality rather than a transmitted message is an interpretation of these passages, not a separately stated mechanism.

passages.heading: 1-jeevan-knowledge-and-the-human-joint-form
passages.section: 1. Jeevan, Knowledge, and the human joint form
passages.text: Five faculties of jeevan, their paired activities, embodied expression, and the field of participation

passages.heading: 1-jeevan-knowledge-and-the-human-joint-form
passages.section: 1. Jeevan, Knowledge, and the human joint form
passages.text: The body is indispensable without being the knower. Body, heart, and prana are described as the gross body; mun, vritti, and chitta as the subtle body; buddhi and atma as the causal body, where “body” in the latter two cases names activity rather than anatomy. Prana joins gross and subtle activity, while chitta joins subtle and causal activity (MVD, pp. 204–205). At the outer relation, sensory motion reaches medhas, and a wave bearing the effect of mun participates in bodily activity and behaviour (MVD, pp. 199–200). These passages identify stages and connections but do not explain why a particular sentient content corresponds to a particular neural process.

passages.heading: 1-jeevan-knowledge-and-the-human-joint-form
passages.section: 1. Jeevan, Knowledge, and the human joint form
passages.text: The distinction is consequently not between an immaterial spectator and a mechanical body. The human being knows, speaks, works, behaves, evaluates, and participates as a joint form. Jeevan bears knowing and acquired orientation; the body supplies the present conditions and means through which they can become observable conduct.

passages.heading: 2-five-faculties-and-ten-paired-activities
passages.section: 2. Five faculties and ten paired activities
passages.text: 2. Five faculties and ten paired activities

passages.heading: 2-five-faculties-and-ten-paired-activities
passages.section: 2. Five faculties and ten paired activities
passages.text: Each faculty has two generic activities. One is classified as bal, an activity in state; the other as shakti, an activity in motion. State here does not mean inactivity, and motion is not restricted to bodily movement. Realisation, enlightenment, contemplation, deliberation, and taste are active ways in which a qualitative orientation is established. Authenticity, resolve, visualisation, analysis, and selection are the paired ways in which that orientation becomes effective (JV, pp. 40, 62; MVD, pp. 131, 323).

passages.heading: 2-five-faculties-and-ten-paired-activities
passages.section: 2. Five faculties and ten paired activities
passages.text: Faculty What it concerns Bal: activity in state Shakti: activity in motion Atma Realisation Anubhav: realisation in coexistence Pramanikta: authenticity and evidence Buddhi Definiteness Bodh: enlightenment or definite understanding Sankalp: resolve according to understanding Chitta Meaning and form Chintan: contemplation Chitran: visualisation, image, or plan Vritti Criteria and alternatives Tulan: deliberation Vishleshan: analysis Mun Acceptability and choice Asvadan: taste or valuation Chayan: selection

passages.heading: 2-five-faculties-and-ten-paired-activities
passages.section: 2. Five faculties and ten paired activities
passages.text: The ten belong to one jeevan. They are neither modules that switch independently nor ten deposits of information. Every jeevan has the constitutional activities; awakening changes their effective content, coordination, criteria, and evidence rather than increasing their quantity (MVD, pp. 199, 275; JV, p. 73).

passages.heading: 2-five-faculties-and-ten-paired-activities
passages.section: 2. Five faculties and ten paired activities
passages.text: 2.1 Atma: realisation and authenticity

passages.heading: 2-five-faculties-and-ten-paired-activities
passages.section: 2. Five faculties and ten paired activities
passages.text: Anubhav is realisation in coexistence rather than episodic sensation. Its paired activity, pramanikta, is authenticity: realised understanding becoming evident. Atma is mediative at the centre, but it does not issue detailed instructions to the other faculties. It supplies the realised orientation with which definite understanding and conduct are to agree (MVD, pp. 211, 323).

passages.heading: 2-five-faculties-and-ten-paired-activities
passages.section: 2. Five faculties and ten paired activities
passages.text: 2.2 Buddhi: enlightenment and resolve

passages.heading: 2-five-faculties-and-ten-paired-activities
passages.section: 2. Five faculties and ten paired activities
passages.text: Bodh is definite understanding, not firmness attached to an assumption. Where meaning remains incorrect or unresolved, bodh concerning that content has not become effective. Beliefs accepted from fear or temptation remain limited to visualisation in chitta; buddhi remains silent until study, enlightenment, and realisation awaken it (MVD, pp. 99–100). Sankalp is resolve based on definiteness. Buddhi can remain alienated from atma, expectational, or unenlightened; the success term bodh should not be confused with every belief attributed to the person (MVD, pp. 216–217, 276, 279).

passages.heading: 2-five-faculties-and-ten-paired-activities
passages.section: 2. Five faculties and ten paired activities
passages.text: 2.3 Chitta: contemplation and visualisation

passages.heading: 2-five-faculties-and-ten-paired-activities
passages.section: 2. Five faculties and ten paired activities
passages.text: Chintan sustains and contemplates meaning. Chitran gives meaning a projectable form: an image, anticipated relationship, explanation, possibility, or plan. The quality of visualisation depends on the meaning it expresses; without enlightenment in truth it necessarily carries excess, deficiency, or omission (MVD, pp. 286, 323).

passages.heading: 2-five-faculties-and-ten-paired-activities
passages.section: 2. Five faculties and ten paired activities
passages.text: 2.4 Vritti: deliberation and analysis

passages.heading: 2-five-faculties-and-ten-paired-activities
passages.section: 2. Five faculties and ten paired activities
passages.text: Tulan deliberates through definite perspectives, while vishleshan distinguishes alternatives, implications, and consequences. The six perspectives are pleasant–unpleasant, healthy–unhealthy, profit–loss, justice–injustice, dharma–adharma, and truth–untruth. Each has its own referent: sensation, body, goods and services, behaviour, resolution, and realisation in existence (MVD, pp. 65–67).

passages.heading: 2-five-faculties-and-ten-paired-activities
passages.section: 2. Five faculties and ten paired activities
passages.text: Pleasure, health, and material result remain relevant in awakened living. Their limitation is that they vary with bodily and material circumstance and cannot finally authorise injustice or contradiction. Justice, dharma, and truth govern them rather than abolish them.

passages.heading: 2-five-faculties-and-ten-paired-activities
passages.section: 2. Five faculties and ten paired activities
passages.text: 2.5 Mun: taste and selection

passages.heading: 2-five-faculties-and-ten-paired-activities
passages.section: 2. Five faculties and ten paired activities
passages.text: Asvadan is the felt assessment of acceptability; chayan selects according to that valuation. Mun is nearest to bodily execution and receives interpreted bodily and sensory conditions through the human joint form. Selection therefore reflects the present organisation of understanding, imagined possibility, deliberative criteria, expectation, bodily condition, and available means (MVD, pp. 204, 323, 327).

passages.heading: 2-five-faculties-and-ten-paired-activities
passages.section: 2. Five faculties and ten paired activities
passages.text: 2.6 Two uses of bal and shakti

passages.heading: 2-five-faculties-and-ten-paired-activities
passages.section: 2. Five faculties and ten paired activities
passages.text: The corpus uses the terms at two grains. At the activity level, state activities are strengths and motion activities powers. At the faculty level, mun, vritti, chitta, buddhi, and atma themselves are called the five strengths, while hope, thought, desire, resoluteness, and evidence or authenticity are called their powers (MVD, pp. 199, 275; SB, pp. 63, 139; AVD, p. 151).

passages.heading: 2-five-faculties-and-ten-paired-activities
passages.section: 2. Five faculties and ten paired activities
passages.text: These formulations are related but not fully reconciled in the texts. The table above adopts the activity-level assignment directly tabulated in AVD, pp. 91–94. It should not be used to erase the faculty-level vocabulary or to infer that every occurrence of bal and shakti names one member of a ten-activity pair.

passages.heading: 3-from-understanding-to-conduct
passages.text: 3. From understanding to conduct

passages.heading: 3-from-understanding-to-conduct
passages.text: The faculties form an ordered architecture, not a production line. Each performs its own activity while becoming consonant with an orientation available inward of it. Two outward sequences help make the account intelligible.

passages.heading: 3-from-understanding-to-conduct
passages.text: The realisation-based sequence runs through the activities in state:

passages.heading: 3-from-understanding-to-conduct
passages.text: realisation → enlightenment → contemplation → deliberation → taste

passages.heading: 3-from-understanding-to-conduct
passages.text: Realisation in atma is followed by enlightenment in buddhi, contemplation in chitta, deliberation of justice, dharma, and truth in vritti, and taste in mun (MVD, pp. 276–277).

passages.heading: 3-from-understanding-to-conduct
passages.text: The paired activities in motion make that organisation effective:

passages.heading: 3-from-understanding-to-conduct
passages.text: authenticity → resolve → visualisation → analysis → selection

passages.heading: 3-from-understanding-to-conduct
passages.text: When selection is embodied, the sequence extends through bodily capacity, speech, work, behaviour, relationship, and material result. This is not the conversion of one activity into another. Each faculty responds through its own pair, and the body and circumstances constrain what can actually be performed.

passages.heading: 3-from-understanding-to-conduct
passages.text: 3.1 Projection and reflection

passages.heading: 3-from-understanding-to-conduct
passages.text: In the directional account used here, paravartan is the outward manifestation of orientation, while pratyavartan is the movement of awakening in which an outer faculty comes to accord with the faculty inward of it. Hope in mun becomes according to thought in vritti; thought according to chitta; desire according to enlightenment in buddhi; and enlightenment according to realisation in atma (MVD, pp. 275–277, 307).

passages.heading: 3-from-understanding-to-conduct
passages.text: The adjoining relations are also named from the content they make effective. Awareness of realisation (pratiti) occurs between buddhi and chitta as contemplation; comprehension (aabhas) between chitta and vritti as deliberation of justice, dharma, and truth; and perception (bhas) between vritti and mun as taste of values with selection and fulfilment of relationships (MVD, pp. 99–100). These are descriptions of coherence among faculties, not three further faculties.

passages.heading: 3-from-understanding-to-conduct
passages.text: The combined form of reflection and projection is the cognisance–sensitivity cycle and the awakened jeevan cycle (MVD, p. 275). Reflection in this directional sense is not a bodily consequence travelling into atma, nor are the state activities simply run backwards. Other source uses are retained in the technical companion §13.

passages.heading: 3-from-understanding-to-conduct
passages.text: The relation between state–motion and projection–reflection remains unsettled. AVD places the bal activities under pratyavartan and the shakti activities under paravartan, while the realisation-based sequence orders the state activities outward. This note therefore does not declare the two distinctions either identical or fully independent.

passages.heading: 3-from-understanding-to-conduct
passages.text: The cycle also bears explanatory weight: lack of understanding of projection, reflection, and their effects is identified with mysteriousness and with movement toward decline despite the wish for awakening (MVD, p. 291). The architecture is therefore meant to make activity knowable, not merely to supply names.

passages.heading: 3-from-understanding-to-conduct
passages.text: 3.2 Receptivity

passages.heading: 3-from-understanding-to-conduct
passages.text: An indication can be available without being received. The ability to receive a higher-conformance indication arises through internal regulation of jeevan’s powers, and four conditions are named (MVD, p. 284).

passages.heading: 3-from-understanding-to-conduct
passages.text: Faculty receiving Condition Supporting influence Mun receiving from vritti Absence of crime Orderliness Vritti receiving from chitta Absence of injustice Societal conduct Chitta receiving from buddhi Absence of attachment Study and sanskar Buddhi receiving from atma Absence of ignorance Inward regulation or dhyan

passages.heading: 3-from-understanding-to-conduct
passages.text: Three conditions depend on social and educative life rather than private introspection alone. Awakening is therefore inseparable from relationship, orderliness, study, and an evidence-bearing human tradition.

passages.heading: 3-from-understanding-to-conduct
passages.text: Reception is described as succeeding or failing in this passage, while capacity and receptivity elsewhere admit of degree (MVD, pp. 142, 248). The texts do not explain how partial reception relates to the stated absence-conditions. They also do not state that the paired shakti activity is “turned inward”; the defensible claim is that internal regulation of the powers enables reception.

passages.heading: 3-from-understanding-to-conduct
passages.text: The surrounding account joins practice to reception: crime-free behaviour is supported by orderliness, just thought by social conduct, dharma-oriented desire by study and good sanskar, and ignorance-free buddhi by inward regulation. Reception and immersion then become evident as happiness, peace, contentment, and bliss (MVD, pp. 282–286). The cycle is thus socially supported and conduct-bearing, not closed inside an isolated individual.

passages.heading: 3-from-understanding-to-conduct
passages.text: 3.3 Consequence, evaluation, and inquiry

passages.heading: 3-from-understanding-to-conduct
passages.text: A bodily or relational result is not already labelled as just, fulfilling, or true. Mun tastes its acceptability; vritti deliberates through the relevant criteria; chitta recognises meaning and relationship; buddhi establishes definiteness where understanding succeeds. Correct intention is insufficient if bodily skill, means, timing, or recognition of the other person is inadequate.

passages.heading: 3-from-understanding-to-conduct
passages.text: A consequence may prompt a question, study, or correction. Curiosity is located at mun, inquiry can be borne, and teaching is organised around the learner’s need and questions (MVD, pp. 77–78, 248, 313–314, 344). The developmental sequence names curiosity in mun, enthusiasm in vritti, delight in chitta, elation and immersion in buddhi, and realisation in atma; it is an inwardly regulated orientation toward awakening, not a fixed response protocol (MVD, pp. 77–78). The stronger printed learning relation is that realisation-oriented conceptions become thought and action, while thought arising through action is instilled again as sanskar through inference (MVD, p. 218).

passages.heading: 3-from-understanding-to-conduct
passages.text: Consider a disagreement over family resources. The relationship is to be fulfilled justly, while material means serve assessed need, prosperity, and right use. Mun registers attraction and discomfort; vritti considers bodily, material, and relational consequences; chitta recognises the relationship and possible form of mutual fulfilment; buddhi establishes whether the proposed course is understood; resolve, visualisation, analysis, and selection organise conduct. The use of resources changes the relationship, and both persons must evaluate whether its values were fulfilled. Remaining contradiction can become material for another inquiry.

passages.heading: 4-restfulness-discord-and-awakening
passages.text: 4. Restfulness, discord, and awakening

passages.heading: 4-restfulness-discord-and-awakening
passages.text: The aim is vishram, restfulness: the eradication of unhappiness and the evidence of resolution under continuing activity, not inactivity or withdrawal (MVD, pp. 68, 78–79). Each faculty is described as more developed than the one outside it. When bodily sensation and hope set the final terms, more developed faculties are asked to conform to less developed ones, producing discord, frustration of effort, and thirst for restfulness (MVD, pp. 91, 276).

passages.heading: 4-restfulness-discord-and-awakening
passages.text: In awakening the direction of accord is reversed: mun is immersed through vritti, vritti through chitta, chitta through buddhi, and buddhi through atma. Their functions attain effective capacity through satisfaction, and bodily sensation comes under cognisance (MVD, p. 277).

passages.heading: 4-restfulness-discord-and-awakening
passages.text: 4.1 One immersion, four values

passages.heading: 4-restfulness-discord-and-awakening
passages.text: Realisation in Omnipresence has one effect and flow, named according to the faculty at which it is present:

passages.heading: 4-restfulness-discord-and-awakening
passages.text: Relation Value Buddhi in concurrence with atma Bliss Chitta in concurrence with buddhi Contentment Vritti in concurrence with chitta Peace Mun in concurrence with vritti Happiness

passages.heading: 4-restfulness-discord-and-awakening
passages.text: The same four are described both as one immersion reaching the four outer faculties and as the values arising from concurrence between adjoining faculties (MVD, pp. 307, 327). They are not four rewards to be maximised separately. Bodily pleasure can coexist with discord, and inward calm cannot substitute for failed relationship.

passages.heading: 4-restfulness-discord-and-awakening
passages.text: The four are the inward segment of a wider concurrence account. Just behaviour and vocation bear coexistence and prosperity; body–heart concurrence bears satisfaction; heart–prana concurrence health and growth; prana–mun concurrence strength and motivation; the four faculty relations then bear happiness through bliss; and atma is eternally in coexistence with Omnipresence, bearing ultimate bliss (MVD, p. 327). These outer and innermost terms should not be collapsed into four additional values of jeevan.

passages.heading: 4-restfulness-discord-and-awakening
passages.text: 4.2 Delusion and the four and a half activities

passages.heading: 4-restfulness-discord-and-awakening
passages.text: In delusion, selection and taste operate in mun; analysis and deliberation toward pleasure, health, and profit in vritti; and visualisation in chitta. These are the four and a half effective activities (MVD, pp. 79, 89; JV, p. 73). The half is deliberation restricted to the first three perspectives. Its result does not become contemplation in chitta, so contemplation is absent rather than half-effective (AVD, p. 152). Mun’s two generic activities are therefore already effective; they occupy a sensory and bodily field. The sixty-four detailed activities of mun are not a second list that remains off until awakening (§6).

passages.heading: 4-restfulness-discord-and-awakening
passages.text: Delusion can therefore be imaginative, analytical, skilled, and socially successful. Its limitation is not lack of activity but the criteria and depth that govern it. The body is taken as the self, sensation and material result set the final terms, and buddhi and atma do not effectively orient conduct.

passages.heading: 4-restfulness-discord-and-awakening
passages.text: Awakening does not install new activities. It brings knowing and believing into relation with recognising and fulfilling, allowing all ten activities to become evident in behaviour (JV, p. 74). Intermediate statuses are specified by which inward faculty effectively orients the outer activity (MVD, pp. 278–279).

passages.heading: 4-restfulness-discord-and-awakening
passages.text: Status Effective orientation Partially awakened Mun and vritti are driven by chitta: desire organises thought and hope Half-awakened Mun, vritti, and chitta are driven by buddhi, but resolve is without atma-bodh Awakened or completely awakened Resolve is with atma-bodh; atma regulates and disciplines buddhi, chitta, vritti, and mun

passages.heading: 4-restfulness-discord-and-awakening
passages.text: These are gradations of effective orientation, not different kinds of jeevan.

passages.heading: 4-restfulness-discord-and-awakening
passages.text: 4.3 Capacity without additional power

passages.heading: 4-restfulness-discord-and-awakening
passages.text: Constitutional capacity and effective capacity must remain distinct. Jeevan’s provision of strength and power is complete and inexhaustible; awakening does not add a quantity of power. What develops is clarity, receptivity, coordination, criterion, skill, and evidential reach.

passages.heading: 4-restfulness-discord-and-awakening
passages.text: Capacity, ability, and receptivity—kshamata, yogyata, and patrata—are distributed in the complete development of chitta, vritti, and mun: creative visualisation according to buddhi, thought of dharma according to chitta, and receptivity for just behaviour according to vritti (MVD, pp. 322–323). Their corresponding roles at buddhi and atma are not named in the same three-term form.

passages.heading: 4-restfulness-discord-and-awakening
passages.text: 4.4 The practical fields of knowledge

passages.heading: 4-restfulness-discord-and-awakening
passages.text: The faculties and activities operate upon known content; that content is not another set of faculties. The printed sources distinguish four bodily propensities—eating, sleeping, protection, and mating—and five sensory modalities: sound, touch, visible form, taste, and smell. They group resolution with the wealth, progeny, and public-recognition motives (vitteshana, putreshana, and lokeshana) as intellectual satisfaction, and separately describe upakar as help and inspiration for another’s prosperity and awakening (MVD, pp. 58, 64–65, 73).

passages.heading: 4-restfulness-discord-and-awakening
passages.text: These fields differ by what is being fulfilled. Bodily and sensory information serves bodily maintenance and interaction; the eshanas become humane responsibilities under resolution, justice, and right use; upakar employs resolved capacity to support another’s material sufficiency and awakening while preserving mutuality. The four propensities and three eshanas have distinct points of effect in the activity architecture (MVD, pp. 203–205, 305).

passages.heading: 4-restfulness-discord-and-awakening
passages.text: An oral schema reportedly groups four bodily propensities, four sensory activities, three eshanas, and upakar as twelve practical knowledges. No located source enumerates that set or names the four sensory activities, so §7 records it as unfinished source work rather than using it to organise the account.

passages.heading: 5-sanskar-learning-and-continuity
passages.text: 5. Sanskar, learning, and continuity

passages.heading: 5-sanskar-learning-and-continuity
passages.text: Sanskar is acquired orientation toward completeness: understood content, acceptance, valuation, responsibility, participation, and readiness for conduct. It is shaped through environment, study, practice, prior organisation, work, behaviour, and evaluation (MVD, pp. 90, 121, 134; JV, pp. 49–50). It is not merely information remembered in chitta, genetic inheritance, or a database located in one faculty.

passages.heading: 5-sanskar-learning-and-continuity
passages.text: The sentient aspect’s sanskar is described as attained awakening in mun, vritti, chitta, and buddhi (MVD, p. 121). This supports reading it as organisation across those four faculties. Treating atma as realised orientation rather than a fifth store is an interpretive distinction, since the passages do not provide a theory of storage or explicitly settle whether awakening of the four includes atma implicitly.

passages.heading: 5-sanskar-learning-and-continuity
passages.text: 5.1 Knowing, believing, recognising, and fulfilling

passages.heading: 5-sanskar-learning-and-continuity
passages.text: A more source-near description avoids the language of stored state. The entirety of human sanskar is presented as knowing, believing or accepting, recognising, and fulfilling (SB, p. 237). Knowing and believing belong to cognisance; recognising and fulfilling to sensitivity held under cognisance (KD §3.4, p. 66). Awakening joins these activities where deluded living had evidenced only recognising and fulfilling sensory desires (JV, p. 74).

passages.heading: 5-sanskar-learning-and-continuity
passages.text: These four terms explain why information alone is insufficient. What is known must be accepted through understanding, recognised in the present relationship and circumstance, fulfilled through competent embodied activity, and evaluated in its result. Repetition can increase skill without establishing knowledge if its criterion remains sensation, approval, or assumption.

passages.heading: 5-sanskar-learning-and-continuity
passages.text: 5.2 Evidence and transmission

passages.heading: 5-sanskar-learning-and-continuity
passages.text: The primary evidence chain runs from realisation into conduct and human tradition:

passages.heading: 5-sanskar-learning-and-continuity
passages.text: Realisation itself is the ultimate evidence, evidence itself is the understanding or knowledge, understanding itself is manifest, the manifest itself is resolution, work and behaviour, work and behaviour itself is evidence, evidence itself is awakened tradition, awakened tradition itself is coexistence. (MVD, p. 12)

passages.heading: 5-sanskar-learning-and-continuity
passages.text: Comprehension is also evidenced in the ability to convey understanding to another (JV, p. 26). Sanskar is described as given by an awakened tradition, imparted through education-sanskar, embraced, and evidenced (MVD, pp. 121, 344; SB, p. 237). No passage describes mechanical copying between jeevans. Explanation supplies language, definition, and indication for another jeevan to examine, understand, practise, and evidence; the teacher–learner relation remains inquiry-bearing and participatory.

passages.heading: 5-sanskar-learning-and-continuity
passages.text: Evaluation remains part of evidence. Justice includes recognition of relationship, fulfilment of its values, evaluation, and mutual satisfaction (MVD, pp. 310–311, 336). A person may state a correct value yet misrecognise the relationship, lack the ability or means to fulfil it, or mistake unilateral satisfaction for mutual fulfilment.

passages.heading: 5-sanskar-learning-and-continuity
passages.text: 5.3 Bodily death and later embodiment

passages.heading: 5-sanskar-learning-and-continuity
passages.text: Jeevan continues after bodily death and later associates with another body. Where understanding and satisfaction have been attained, their established condition continues because jeevan does not die (JV, pp. 20, 55, 77). Bodily death therefore ends the present gross means of expression; it does not end jeevan’s activity or create a new sentient unit. Without a gross body, subtle activities are said to occur according to the indication of buddhi (KD, p. 31).

passages.heading: 5-sanskar-learning-and-continuity
passages.text: The later bodily association is placed from about the fourth or fifth month of pregnancy (JV, p. 94). Acceptances toward completeness and knowledge, wisdom, and science moving toward resolution are said to be carried forward as prarabdh; prarabdh also names the difference between what can be known, desired, done, and undergone—what remains to be undergone (MVD, pp. 90–91). Neither formulation supplies a rule matching one jeevan to one body. The sources do not state that every analytical component of acquired organisation is preserved without change or provide a public method for separating earlier organisation from present education, bodily condition, relationship, circumstance, and choice. Explicit autobiographical recall is also not stated as the form in which continuity must appear.

passages.heading: 6-the-sixty-one-pairs-and-122-activities
passages.text: 6. The sixty-one pairs and 122 activities

passages.heading: 6-the-sixty-one-pairs-and-122-activities
passages.text: The ten generic activities are refined into 122 detailed activities. Their distribution is stated as

passages.heading: 6-the-sixty-one-pairs-and-122-activities
passages.text: Faculty locus Pairs Activities Generic pair Atma, nucleus 1 2 Realisation–authenticity Buddhi, first orbit 2 4 Enlightenment–resolve Chitta, second orbit 8 16 Contemplation–visualisation Vritti, third orbit 18 36 Deliberation–analysis Mun, fourth orbit 32 64 Taste–selection Total 61 122 State–motion

passages.heading: 6-the-sixty-one-pairs-and-122-activities
passages.text: The counts and identity with state and motion are given at MVD, p. 323; the activities are defined at pp. 328–348; and AVD, pp. 91–94, tabulates every member in a bal or shakti column. The first member of every paired heading in the definitions agrees with the bal column and the second with the shakti column.

passages.heading: 6-the-sixty-one-pairs-and-122-activities
passages.text: The enumeration supplies a source-governed assignment, not one relation repeated sixty-one times. The definitions include accepted states and readiness for expression, held conditions and their evidence, relationships with associated values or responsibilities, an activity and what it bears, acts and objects, and sensory qualities with varied correlates. No one relation covers all sixty-one, and the classification cannot be reconstructed from which definition sounds more static.

passages.heading: 6-the-sixty-one-pairs-and-122-activities
passages.text: The detailed inventory, translation variants, non-uniform pair relations, missing sound pair, and unresolved derivation of the counts are kept in The Sixty-One Activity Pairs of Jeevan. The sixty-one pairs are contents of the five generic pairs: what each faculty establishes as bal, and how the paired shakti makes that establishment effective. They are not sixty-one further faculties, variables, or independently switchable functions, and they are not “dimensions” in the source’s sense—the eight dimensions of visualisation are a separate list and are not mapped onto chitta’s eight pairs (MVD, p. 327).

passages.heading: 6-the-sixty-one-pairs-and-122-activities
passages.text: The 122 are tabulated as conducts of awakened jeevan (AVD, p. 91). In delusion, mun’s taste and selection already operate, mainly over sensation and bodily use; the four and a half are sufficient for the five senses and four instincts (JV, pp. 73–74; §4.2). The thirty-two mun pairs name the awakened inventory of those two activities. They do not remain unused from lack of need, and a row is not the selection of its bal member.

passages.heading: 7-source-status-and-open-work
passages.text: 7. Source status and open work

passages.heading: 7-source-status-and-open-work
passages.text: The architecture has four evidential levels.

passages.heading: 7-source-status-and-open-work
passages.text: Directly stated: the constitution of jeevan; five faculties; ten and 122 activities; activity-level state and motion; the directional order of awakening; reception conditions; four values; four-and-a-half activities; bodily and unembodied stages; and continuity across bodily death.

passages.heading: 7-source-status-and-open-work
passages.text: Cross-text synthesis: the concise faculty descriptions in §2; the two outward sequences in §3; sanskar as organisation distributed across four faculties; intermediate awakening as increasing effective depth; the term-for-term correspondence between immersion and adjoining concurrence; and the 122 as contents of the ten rather than a second on/off list.

passages.heading: 7-source-status-and-open-work
passages.text: Technical interpretation: optional notation for relating present activity, acquired orientation, receptivity, inquiry, embodied consequence, evidence, and continuity across embodiments. These proposals are explicitly labelled in the technical companion.

passages.heading: 7-source-status-and-open-work
passages.text: Oral or presently weak: a twelvefold practical schema composed of four bodily propensities, four sensory activities, three eshanas, and upakar. The four bodily propensities, three eshanas, and upakar are attested individually, while no consulted printed passage or repository recording enumerates the twelve or names four sensory activities. The five sensory modalities are repeatedly attested. The twelvefold should therefore not organise the reader account or constrain the technical model until its source is located.

passages.heading: 7-source-status-and-open-work
passages.text: Five groups of questions remain: the relation between sentient content and bodily mediation; the several uses of bal–shakti and projection–reflection; the process joining consequence, inquiry, corrected understanding, and lasting sanskar; the public evidence for mutual satisfaction and continuity across embodiments; and the unresolved derivation, pair relations, sensory omissions, and oral schema surrounding the 122 activities. The full research agenda is in the technical companion §12.

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: Editorial Notes

passages.heading: editorial-notes
passages.text: The reader follows the activity-level bal–shakti assignment in AVD, the directional cycle in MVD, and the four-faculty placement of attained sanskar without claiming that the corresponding variants have been harmonised. The unused textual variants, overlapping terms, and excluded oral schema are documented in the technical companion §13; pair-level variants remain in the inventory §8.
